sections.h2: Does Arkansas sell tax liens or tax deeds?
sections.html:
The statutes and rules describe the sale of the land itself by a state officer, and they bar sales by the county. Under Ark. Code 26-37-101, tax-delinquent land cannot be sold at the county level.

The county collector holds the delinquency for a year. If the owner has not redeemed by the certification date, the collector sends the parcel to the Commissioner of State Lands, who collects the taxes or sells the property at public auction. A buyer at that sale receives a deed from the state, not a certificate that earns interest, so the rest of this page follows the deed path.

sections.h2: What is the timeline from missed payment to state auction?
sections.html:
More than two years can pass between the missed due date and a sale, because the state receives the parcel about a year after the due date and a sale cannot come earlier than one year after that. The steps below come from 26-37-101 and the Commissioner's rules.

StepWhat happens
October 15Taxes become delinquent
One year laterCounty collector holds, then certifies the land after notice
By July 1 of the next yearLatest certification date
On receipt of certificationTitle vests in the State of Arkansas, in care of the Commissioner
At least 30 days before saleCertified mail notice of the sale and the right to redeem
At least 60 days before sale (homestead)Personal service if there is no proof of receiving the mail
At least 1 year after certificationEarliest sale date

Certification names all taxes, penalties, interest and costs, along with the owner of record and last known address. The Commissioner does not take physical possession and has no duty to maintain the property, so upkeep of the house stays with whoever occupies it.

sections.h2: Who must be notified before the sale?
sections.html:
The owner and the interested parties of record must be notified, first by certified mail. Section 26-37-301 sets the notice rules, and the Commissioner's rules add a newspaper publication.

  • If the certified mail comes back unclaimed or refused, the Commissioner resends by regular mail.
  • If it is undelivered for another reason, a second notice goes to any other address in county property records, such as the one on the deed or a forwarding address held by the collector or assessor.
  • For joint tenants every owner counts, and for tenants by the entirety either spouse counts.
  • A homestead owner who cannot be shown to have received the mail is served in person at least 60 days before the sale, and that owner pays the extra cost.

The notice gives a short legal description, the parcel number, the sale date and a warning that the land will be sold unless redeemed. The notice goes to the owner of record at the last known address, so an heir who never updated the records may not see it. Only a person who did not receive notice in substantial compliance can challenge it.

sections.h2: How do you redeem tax-delinquent land?
sections.html:
Pay the taxes, penalties, interest and costs, with a petition, before 4:00 p.m. Central on the last business day before the sale. The Commissioner's real estate division accepts payment online through its Pay Taxes button, or by check or money order with a signed petition to redeem.

  • You need the parcel number from your tax bill.
  • Partial or incorrect payments are rejected and do not extend the deadline.
  • A quoted payoff stays valid for 30 days.
  • Anyone may redeem, and redeeming does not change who owns the property.

The division's phone is 501-324-9422, and its office is at 7003 Valley Ranch Drive in Little Rock. A redemption deed is issued when the payoff is made, and a receipt goes to a redeemer who is not the record owner.

Parcels first go to a public in-person auction, and any that do not sell move to an online auction about 30 days later. The Commissioner's rules, in the 2023 edition on Cornell's site, set out the bidding terms.

  • Bidders register, get a bid card and show photo identification.
  • The highest bid at or above the minimum wins, and an accepted oral bid is binding.
  • Payment is due at the sale by check, certified funds or card. Cash and installment plans are not accepted.
  • Online, the winner pays $100 earnest money, or the whole bid if it is under $100, and the balance in certified funds within 10 business days.
  • State staff, the county collector or deputy, foreign-address entities, and former owners or interested parties cannot bid.

The bar on former owners matters to sellers. Once a house reaches auction, the owner cannot buy it back at the sale. Redemption before the sale is the only route to keep it.

sections.h2: What does the winning bidder actually get?
sections.html:
A limited warranty deed that conveys only the State's interest, and the rules note that it often requires a court action to quiet title. The deed is issued after full payment and recorded with the county.

The Commissioner's rules also describe a 90-day litigation period. That means a buyer at the state's sale receives less than an ordinary seller would convey. For parcels that go unsold at the first auction, the online reserve bid equals the taxes and costs for the first two years, a figure tied to the debt and not to the house's value.

Money bid above taxes, fees, penalties, interest and costs is excess proceeds. The rules pay the Commissioner's costs and the county's taxes first, then other government claims, and send the remainder to the former owner, less up to $500 for administration. Claims are denied unless every requirement is met strictly, and the rules show some inconsistency on the claim period, so check the current rule before counting on a timeline.

sections.h2: What else shows up on the way to certification?
sections.html:
The county collector publishes lists before the state ever sees the parcel. Craighead County's page says the collector prepares a list of delinquent personal property taxes before December 1 each year for a legal newspaper, which must publish it within seven days, and that delinquent real estate taxes are listed in a local newspaper after the deadline.

The Commissioner's division also keeps the county certification books and researches the title of each certified parcel before it notifies owners and interested parties. Each of those is a point where an owner can still catch the problem and pay the county or the state. The sooner a payoff is requested, the fewer months of penalty and interest it carries.

  • Check the newspaper list in your county after October 15.
  • Keep the mailing address on the tax bill current.
  • Look up the parcel number on your latest tax bill before calling any office.

sections.h2: Can you sell the house before it is certified or sold?
sections.html:
Yes, a sale at any point before the auction takes the parcel out of the process once the taxes are paid. Because anyone may redeem, a buyer can pay the redemption amount, and a title company can arrange that payoff from the sale proceeds.

  • Before certification: pay the county collector, and the title company can take the payoff from the sale proceeds.
  • After certification: request a payoff from the Commissioner by parcel number, and note the 30 day quote window.
  • Close before the cutoff, which is 4:00 p.m. Central the last business day before the sale.

Cash Home Buyers makes as-is offers on Arkansas houses with back taxes. Keep your parcel number and the sale date from your notice at hand, because the cutoff time controls what is possible.

faqs.q: Can the county sell my house for unpaid taxes in Arkansas?
faqs.a: No. Section 26-37-101 says tax-delinquent land cannot be sold at the county level. The county certifies it to the Commissioner of State Lands, and the state sells it at auction.

faqs.q: When does the state take title?
faqs.a: When the Commissioner receives the county's certification, which must happen by July 1 of the year after the one-year delinquency period. Title vests in the State of Arkansas, in care of the Commissioner.

faqs.q: What is the last moment to redeem?
faqs.a: 4:00 p.m. Central on the last business day before the auction. Partial payments are rejected and do not extend the deadline.

faqs.q: Can I bid on my own house at the auction?
faqs.a: No. The Commissioner's rules bar former owners and interested parties from bidding.

faqs.q: Do I get the extra money if the house sells for more than I owe?
faqs.a: Possibly. Excess proceeds go first to the Commissioner's costs, the county's taxes and other government claims, then to the former owner minus up to $500 for administration, but you must file a claim that meets every requirement.

faqs.q: Does redeeming transfer ownership to the person who pays?
faqs.a: No. The Commissioner's division states that redeeming does not change ownership, and anyone may pay on a parcel.
